Abstract—We present a way to lift up the Tower complexity
lower bound of the reachability problem for Petri nets to
match the Ackermannian upper bound closing a long standing
open problem. We also prove that the reachability problem in
dimension 17 is not elementary.
Keywords-Petri nets; reachability; complexity; fast growing
functions;

Petri nets, or equivalent models like the checking programs introduced in this paper are systems acting on counters ranging over the natural numbers thanks to increment,
decrement, and test commands (only at the end of an
execution). The central algorithmic problem for checking
programs is reachability: given a checking program, decide
whether there exists an execution from an initial conﬁguration to a ﬁnal one. Many important computational problems
in logic and complexity reduce or are even equivalent to
this problem [1, 2]. After an incomplete proof by Sacerdote
and Tenney [3], decidability of the problem was established by Mayr [4, 5], whose proof was then simpliﬁed by
Kosaraju [6]. Building on the further reﬁnements made by
Lambert in the 1990s [7], in 2015, a ﬁrst complexity upper
bound of the reachability problem was provided [8] more
than thirty years after the presentation of the algorithm introduced by Mayr [6, 7]. The upper bound given in that paper is
“cubic Ackermannian”, i.e. in Fω3 (see [9]). This complexity
bound is obtained by analyzing the Mayr algorithm. With a
reﬁned algorithm and a new ranking function for proving
termination, an Ackermannian complexity upper bound was
obtained [10]. This means that the reachability problem can
be solved in time bounded by A(p(n)) where p is a primitive
recursive function and where A is the Ackermann function.
This paper also showed that the reachability problem in ﬁxed
dimension d (the dimension is the number of used counters)
is primitive recursive by bounding the length of executions
by O(Fd+4 (n)) where Fd+4 is a primitive recursive function
of the Grzegorczyk hierarchy (see Section I for the deﬁnition
of those functions), and n is the size of the input.
Concerning the complexity lower bound, in 1976,
the reachability problem was proved to be EXPSPACEhard [11]. This bound used to be the best one for more
than forty years until 2019 when it was improved to a
Tower complexity lower bound [12], i.e. a non elementary
complexity.

This paper provides the last piece leading to the exact
complexity of the reachability problem for checking programs. As previously mentioned, it follows a long series of
results. This piece of work is not the most difﬁcult one but
it is an important one since it closes a long standing open
problem. Technically, the most difﬁcult piece is the notion

of an execution the tests commands of a Minsky machine
(a machine like a VASS but with commands that can test to

In this paper, we provide several gadgets for implementing

and independently, other gadgets for implementing such an

X. C ONCLUSION
This paper proves that the reachability problem for checking programs is Ackermann-complete. This lower bound
improves the known lower bounds of the reachability problem for many extensions of vector addition systems with
states (VASS). Exploited the extra-power of those models to
obtain new lower bounds is an open problem. For instance,
in [21] we proved that the termination problem of pushdown
VASS is decidable in hyper-Ackermannian complexity, but
we just have elementary lower bounds for that problem.
The techniques introduced in this paper may provide a way
to improve the complexity lower bound of that problem,
but also the complexity lower bound for other problems on
various VASS extensions like the branching VASS and the
data nets.
